meta.title: International Trade Finance
meta.description: Question bank covering cross-border trade risks, Incoterms, documents, letters of credit, collections, financing methods, and trade governing bodies. Designed for the ITF course.

modules.title: Introduction to International Trade (Risks, Payment Methods, Incoterms)
Documentary Letter of Credit (L/C Types, Dynamics, Risks, Discrepancies)
Trade Governing Bodies (WTO, UNCTAD, ICC, AfCFTA)

questionBank.q: An exporter in Germany receives a confirmed order from a buyer in Nigeria. The exporter is concerned about the buyer's ability to pay due to recent foreign exchange restrictions in Nigeria. Which risk is the exporter primarily facing?
opts: A. Performance risk
B. Payment risk
C. Transaction risk
D. Political risk
questionBank.exp: Payment risk is the risk that the exporter may not receive payment due to the buyer's inability to fund or the importing country's policy restricting fund transfers. This is a classic payment risk scenario. (Module 1.1, Risk in Trade Finance)

questionBank.q: A Nigerian importer has contracted with a Chinese supplier for specialised machinery. The supplier has a poor track record of delivering on time. The importer is most concerned about:
opts: A. Country risk
B. Payment risk
C. Performance risk
D. Sovereign risk
questionBank.exp: Performance risk is the risk that the exporter may not deliver goods at all, or deliver goods that do not conform to the contract. Given the supplier's poor track record, this is the primary concern. (Module 1.1)

questionBank.q: A European bank is considering financing an import transaction into a country that has experienced political unrest and frequent changes in trade policy. Which risk category should the bank weigh most heavily?
opts: A. Credit risk
B. Market risk
C. Political/Country risk
D. Operational risk
questionBank.exp: Political/Country risk relates to the political environment, its stability, and its policies regarding cross-border trade. Unrest and policy changes are direct indicators of elevated country risk. (Module 1.1)

questionBank.q: An exporter has shipped goods under a collection instruction that requires the buyer to accept a Bill of Exchange before documents are released. The buyer refuses to accept the draft despite the goods being in transit. Which risk materialises?
opts: A. Transfer risk
B. Non-Acceptance risk
C. Documentation risk
D. Sovereign risk
questionBank.exp: Non-Acceptance risk is specifically the risk that the buyer will not accept the bill of exchange in a collection scenario. This is a distinct risk category. (Module 1.1)

questionBank.q: A seller has delivered goods to a buyer in a foreign country. The buyer has the local currency to pay, but the central bank has suspended foreign currency transfers. The seller faces:
opts: A. Payment risk
B. Transfer risk
C. Legal risk
D. Transaction risk
questionBank.exp: Transfer risk involves the physical movement of funds from the paying country to the receiving country. Even when the buyer has local funds, if the country lacks foreign currency for transfer, the risk crystallises. (Module 1.1)

questionBank.q: An exporter ships goods to a government entity in a developing country. The government defaults on payment due to budget constraints. This is an example of:
opts: A. Country risk
B. Sovereign risk
C. Performance risk
D. Political risk
questionBank.exp: Sovereign risk is a specific sub-category of risk associated with direct lending or transactions with a government entity. It is considered less risky than general country risk. (Module 1.1)

questionBank.q: A bank has received documents under a Letter of Credit that require a Certificate of Origin. The beneficiary submits a certificate that is not in the format required by the importing country's customs. The bank should identify this as:
opts: A. Legal risk
B. Documentation risk
C. Transaction risk
D. Non-Acceptance risk
questionBank.exp: Documentation risk is associated with the specific documentation required for importation. Incorrect or missing documents can lead to refusal or delay, so this is a documentation risk issue. (Module 1.1)

questionBank.q: When two parties from different legal systems enter into a trade contract and a dispute arises over which country's law applies, which risk is most relevant?
opts: A. Legal risk
B. Country risk
C. Political risk
D. Sovereign risk
questionBank.exp: Legal risk is the risk that in case of non-performance by either party, the determination of applicable jurisdiction may be uncertain or unfavourable. The UCP and URC provide guidelines but cannot eliminate jurisdictional issues entirely. (Module 1.1)

questionBank.q: An importer has ordered goods from a new supplier. The goods are shipped but are damaged during a storm at sea. The importer bears this loss if the Incoterm used was:
opts: A. CIF
B. FOB
C. DDP
D. EXW
questionBank.exp: Under FOB, the risk of loss or damage to the goods passes when the goods are on board the vessel. The buyer bears all costs and risks from that moment onward. Therefore, the importer bears the loss during sea transit. (Module 1.3, Incoterms 2020)

questionBank.q: A seller has agreed to deliver goods to the buyer's premises, fully cleared for import and with all duties paid. The appropriate Incoterm is:
opts: A. DAP
B. DDP
C. DPU
D. CIF
questionBank.exp: DDP (Delivered Duty Paid) represents the maximum obligation for the seller. The seller delivers the goods cleared for import, ready for unloading at the named place, and bears all costs and risks including import duties. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: Which of the following Incoterms requires the seller to unload the goods at the buyer's destination?
opts: A. DAP
B. DPU
C. DDP
D. CIF
questionBank.exp: DPU (Delivered at Place Unloaded) is the only Incoterm that obligates the seller to unload goods at the buyer's destination. Under DAP and DDP, the goods are on the arriving means of transport and the buyer unloads. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: An exporter in India sells goods to a buyer in Nigeria under FCA terms. The exporter delivers the goods to the carrier nominated by the buyer at the exporter's warehouse. The carrier then issues a Bill of Lading with an 'On Board' notation. Under Incoterms 2020, which statement is correct?
opts: A. The seller cannot obtain an 'On Board' Bill of Lading under FCA because risk has already passed
B. The seller may request an 'On Board' Bill of Lading from the carrier to satisfy bank requirements
C. The seller must pay for the insurance until the goods are on board
D. The seller is responsible for clearing the goods for import
questionBank.exp: Incoterms 2020 updated FCA to allow the seller to receive an 'On Board' Bill of Lading after delivering goods to the transporter. This helps sellers satisfy bank requirements for letters of credit. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: Under CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid To), what level of insurance cover must the seller obtain?
opts: A. Minimum cover (Institute Cargo Clause C)
B. All-risk cover (Institute Cargo Clause A)
C. No insurance required
D. Cover determined by the buyer
questionBank.exp: Under Incoterms 2020, for CIP shipments, the appropriate insurance clause is Institute Cargo Clause A (all-risk cover). This is a change from previous versions where CIP required only minimum cover. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: Under CIF (Cost, Insurance and Freight), the minimum required insurance cover is:
opts: A. Institute Cargo Clause A
B. Institute Cargo Clause B
C. Institute Cargo Clause C
D. No specified requirement
questionBank.exp: For CIF shipments, the appropriate cover is Institute Cargo Clause C (minimum cover). This contrasts with CIP which now requires Clause A. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A seller in South Africa agrees to deliver goods to a buyer in Kenya under CPT (Carriage Paid To) terms. The seller contracts with a carrier and pays for carriage to Nairobi. When does the risk of loss pass from seller to buyer?
opts: A. When the goods reach Nairobi
B. When the goods are handed over to the first carrier
C. When the goods are on board the vessel
D. When the goods are unloaded in Nairobi
questionBank.exp: Under CPT, CIP, CFR, and CIF, the seller fulfills its obligation when it hands the goods over to the carrier, not when the goods reach the destination. Risk passes at that point. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A buyer in the USA purchases goods from a seller in China under EXW terms. The seller has placed the goods at its warehouse. Which party is responsible for loading the goods onto the truck and arranging export clearance?
opts: A. The seller
B. The buyer
C. The carrier
D. Both parties share equally
questionBank.exp: Under EXW (Ex Works), the seller places the goods at the disposal of the buyer at the seller's premises. The seller does not need to load the goods or clear them for export. The buyer bears all risks and costs from that point, including loading and export clearance. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: An exporter in Germany and an importer in Brazil agree on FOB Hamburg. The goods are loaded on board the vessel at Hamburg. During the voyage, the vessel encounters heavy weather and the goods are damaged. Who bears the loss?
opts: A. The seller, because the goods were damaged before arrival
B. The buyer, because risk passed when the goods were on board
C. The carrier, because they are liable for all damages
D. The insurance company, regardless of Incoterm
questionBank.exp: Under FOB, the risk of loss passes when the goods are on board the vessel at the named port of shipment. Any damage after that point is the buyer's risk (subject to insurance). (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: Which Incoterm imposes the maximum obligation on the seller, including import clearance and duty payment?
opts: A. DAP
B. DDP
C. CIF
D. DDU
questionBank.exp: DDP is the only Incoterm that requires the seller to clear the goods for import, pay import duties, and carry out all customs formalities — representing the seller's maximum obligation. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A seller in the UK ships machinery to a buyer in Nigeria under CFR Apapa. The seller's responsibility includes:
opts: A. Paying for insurance to cover the goods during transit
B. Contracting for and paying the freight to Apapa
C. Clearing the goods for import in Nigeria
D. Unloading the goods at Apapa
questionBank.exp: Under CFR, the seller must contract for and pay the costs and freight necessary to bring the goods to the named port of destination. Insurance is not included (unlike CIF). (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A buyer in Canada agrees to purchase goods from a seller in Vietnam under FCA (Free Carrier). The seller delivers the goods to the carrier at the seller's premises. The buyer has arranged the main carriage. Which party is responsible for loading the goods onto the truck?
opts: A. The seller, because delivery occurs when the goods are placed at the buyer's disposal
B. The buyer, because FCA requires the buyer to load
C. The seller, if delivery is at the seller's premises
D. The carrier, automatically
questionBank.exp: Under FCA, if delivery takes place at the seller's premises, the seller is responsible for loading the goods onto the collecting vehicle. If delivery is at another place, the seller must deliver the goods to the carrier's vehicle without loading. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: Which of the following Incoterms can be used for any mode of transport, including multimodal?
opts: A. FAS
B. FOB
C. CFR
D. CPT
questionBank.exp: CPT (Carriage Paid To) is a rule for any mode of transport, including multimodal. FAS, FOB, and CFR are specific to sea and inland waterway transport. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: An exporter in the UAE sells to a buyer in the UK under DAP terms. The goods arrive at the buyer's warehouse in London on the truck. The buyer wants to unload the goods immediately. Who must pay for the unloading?
opts: A. The seller, because DAP includes unloading
B. The buyer, because DAP requires the buyer to unload
C. The seller and buyer share the cost
D. The carrier, by default
questionBank.exp: Under DAP, the seller delivers the goods on the arriving means of transport ready for unloading. The buyer is responsible for unloading. This distinguishes DAP from DPU where the seller unloads. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A contract uses the Incoterm FOB. The seller has arranged for the goods to be loaded on board the vessel. The buyer's bank requires a Bill of Lading showing 'On Board' notation. Who is responsible for obtaining this Bill of Lading?
opts: A. The seller, as the shipper
B. The buyer, as the consignee
C. The carrier, automatically
D. The bank, as the issuing authority
questionBank.exp: Under FOB, the seller delivers the goods on board and procures the goods already so delivered. The seller (shipper) obtains the Bill of Lading from the carrier to prove shipment. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: When a seller and buyer have a well-established, long-term relationship and trust each other, the payment method most likely chosen is:
opts: A. Advance Payment
B. Open Account
C. Documentary Credit
D. Collection
questionBank.exp: Open Account is suitable where a valuable trading relationship exists and trust is high (e.g., between parent and subsidiary, or where credit bureaus are effective). It involves the seller shipping goods and sending an invoice with payment terms. (Module 1.2)

questionBank.q: A seller is exporting to a new buyer in a country with high political instability. The seller wants to eliminate payment risk entirely. The best payment method is:
opts: A. Open Account
B. Advance Payment
C. Documentary Collection
D. Confirmed Letter of Credit
questionBank.exp: A Confirmed Letter of Credit gives the seller the undertaking of both the issuing bank and a confirming bank (usually in the seller's country). This reduces payment risk to near zero for the seller, assuming documents comply. Advance Payment shifts risk to the buyer, so it's not the seller's best option if the seller wants to secure payment while still shipping. (Module 1.2)

questionBank.q: A buyer is concerned that the seller may not ship goods on time or may send inferior quality products. Which payment method gives the buyer the most protection?
opts: A. Advance Payment
B. Open Account
C. Documentary Collection
D. Documentary Credit
questionBank.exp: Under a Documentary Credit, the buyer's bank reviews documents and ensures they comply with terms before payment. The buyer also controls the latest shipment date and can specify quality requirements in the L/C. This gives the buyer the strongest protection against performance risk. (Module 1.2)

questionBank.q: Under a Documentary Collection, the seller ships goods and sends documents to the buyer's bank with instructions. The buyer can obtain the shipping documents only after:
opts: A. The buyer signs a trust receipt
B. The buyer pays or accepts the bill of exchange as per the collection order
C. The buyer receives the goods physically
D. The buyer sends a copy of the commercial invoice
questionBank.exp: In a documentary collection, the seller instructs the banks to release documents against payment (D/P) or acceptance (D/A). The buyer must pay or accept the bill of exchange to obtain the documents, which control the goods. (Module 1.2)

questionBank.q: The 'trust league table' ranks payment methods from least trust to most trust required. The correct order from least trust to most trust is:
opts: A. Open Account, Collection, L/C, Advance Payment
B. Advance Payment, L/C, Collection, Open Account
C. L/C, Advance Payment, Collection, Open Account
D. L/C, Collection, Advance Payment, Open Account
questionBank.exp: The trust league table (from the slides) shows: Advance Payment (least trust in buyer), then L/C, then Collection, then Open Account (most trust). The order is: Payment in advance → Letter of Credit → Bill for Collection → Open account trading. (Module 1.2, METHODS OF PAYMENT section)

questionBank.q: An exporter has received an irrevocable, confirmed Letter of Credit from a Nigerian bank. The exporter is still concerned about political risk in Nigeria. Which action best mitigates this?
opts: A. Requesting an Advance Payment
B. Asking the confirming bank to also cover political risk
C. Accepting only an unconfirmed L/C
D. No action needed because confirmed L/C eliminates all risks
questionBank.exp: A confirmed L/C only covers the credit risk of the issuing bank. Political risk (such as exchange controls or transfer restrictions) is not covered by the L/C itself. Some confirming banks offer political risk insurance or coverage as an additional service. (Module 1.2 and 1.1)

questionBank.q: A buyer in Europe purchases goods from a seller in Asia. The Incoterm agreed is CIF. The seller has arranged insurance but the cargo is lost at sea. The buyer files a claim against the insurance company. Which party originally contracted the insurance?
opts: A. The buyer, because they bear the risk
B. The seller, because CIF requires the seller to obtain insurance
C. The carrier, as it was their vessel
D. The bank, as the intermediary
questionBank.exp: Under CIF, the seller must contract for insurance cover against the buyer's risk of loss or damage during carriage. The seller pays for the insurance and is responsible for making the claim if necessary, but the policy is for the buyer's benefit. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: An exporter in Australia ships goods to a buyer in Japan under FAS (Free Alongside Ship) terms. The goods are placed on the quay next to the vessel. Before loading, a fire damages the goods. Who bears the loss?
opts: A. The seller, because risk passes only when goods are alongside
B. The buyer, because risk passed when goods were alongside the ship
C. The carrier, because the fire occurred at the port
D. The insurance company, regardless
questionBank.exp: Under FAS, the seller delivers when the goods are placed alongside the vessel on the quay or barge. The risk of loss passes at that moment. Since the goods were already alongside, the buyer bears the loss. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: When using the DPU Incoterm, the seller bears all risks up to what point?
opts: A. Until the goods are placed on the vessel
B. Until the goods are unloaded at the named destination
C. Until the goods are delivered to the buyer's warehouse
D. Until the goods are cleared for import
questionBank.exp: Under DPU, the seller bears all risks involved in bringing the goods to and unloading them at the named place of destination. Risk passes after unloading, when the goods are placed at the disposal of the buyer. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A seller in the UK agrees to deliver goods to a buyer in the USA under DAP (Delivered at Place). The goods arrive at the buyer's warehouse but the buyer does not unload them immediately. The seller's responsibility ends:
opts: A. When the goods are unloaded
B. When the goods are placed at the disposal of the buyer on the arriving truck
C. When the goods clear US customs
D. When the buyer pays for the goods
questionBank.exp: Under DAP, the seller delivers when the goods are placed at the disposal of the buyer on the arriving means of transport, ready for unloading at the named place. The buyer is responsible for unloading from that point. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A contract specifies CPT (Carriage Paid To) but the seller is unable to obtain insurance. The buyer insists the seller must obtain insurance because the risk is with the buyer. Which party is correct?
opts: A. The seller, because insurance is mandatory under CPT
B. The buyer, because under CPT the seller must also provide insurance
C. Neither, because CPT does not require the seller to provide insurance
D. Both, because CPT requires mutual insurance
questionBank.exp: Under CPT, the seller must contract for carriage but has no obligation to obtain insurance. This is a key distinction from CIP and CIF. Insurance is the buyer's responsibility under CPT. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: Which of the following Incoterms allows the seller to meet the buyer's bank's requirement for an 'On Board' Bill of Lading while still using a multimodal carrier?
opts: A. FOB
B. FAS
C. FCA
D. CFR
questionBank.exp: Incoterms 2020 updated FCA to allow the seller to receive an 'On Board' multimodal Bill of Lading after delivering goods to the carrier, helping satisfy bank requirements. FOB, FAS, and CFR are sea/waterway-specific and do not fit multimodal carriage as naturally. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: An importer in Ghana agrees to buy goods from a seller in Turkey under EXW. The seller informs the buyer that they will not load the goods onto the buyer's truck. The buyer disputes, claiming the seller is responsible for loading. Who is correct?
opts: A. The seller, because EXW places goods at the buyer's disposal and the buyer must collect them, including loading
B. The buyer, because the seller must assist with loading
C. The carrier, because loading is always their duty
D. The seller, but only if the goods are dangerous
questionBank.exp: Under EXW, the seller does not need to load the goods on any collecting vehicle. The buyer bears all costs and risks from that point, including loading. The seller's obligation is minimal. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A seller in the USA has agreed to ship goods to a buyer in Germany under CIF Bremen. The seller has procured insurance but the goods are lost at sea. The buyer wants to claim from the insurance company but does not have the insurance policy. Who should have provided the insurance policy to the buyer?
opts: A. The seller, because CIF requires the seller to provide the insurance document to the buyer
B. The buyer, because they must arrange their own insurance
C. The carrier, because they are the insured party
D. The bank, because it issued the L/C
questionBank.exp: Under CIF, the seller must contract for insurance and provide the insurance document (policy or certificate) to the buyer, as it is part of the shipping documents. The buyer needs this to claim from the insurer. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A buyer in Brazil and a seller in South Africa agree on CFR Santos. The seller pays the freight. The vessel is delayed and arrives after the expected date. The buyer incurs demurrage charges at the port. Who is liable for the demurrage?
opts: A. The seller, because they arranged carriage
B. The buyer, because risk and costs of unloading are the buyer's responsibility
C. The carrier, because they caused the delay
D. Shared between seller and buyer
questionBank.exp: Under CFR, the seller pays the freight to the named port, but all costs and risks after the goods are on board the vessel are for the buyer's account. Demurrage is a cost at the port of discharge, typically borne by the buyer. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: An exporter in India ships goods to a buyer in the UK under DDP terms. The goods are stopped at the UK border because the seller's paperwork for import is incorrect. The buyer cannot clear the goods. Who bears the additional costs to correct the paperwork?
opts: A. The buyer, because they are the importer of record
B. The seller, because DDP requires the seller to clear for import
C. The carrier, because they are responsible for transport
D. The UK customs authority, because they required the check
questionBank.exp: Under DDP, the seller has an obligation to clear the goods for import and pay any import duty. If the paperwork is incorrect, the seller is responsible for rectifying it and bears any associated costs. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A seller in Nigeria agrees to supply goods to a buyer in Ghana under FCA at the seller's warehouse. The buyer arranges for a truck to collect the goods. The seller loads the goods onto the truck. At what point does the risk pass to the buyer?
opts: A. When the goods are placed at the disposal of the buyer at the warehouse
B. When the goods are loaded onto the truck
C. When the truck leaves the warehouse
D. When the goods reach the border
questionBank.exp: Under FCA, if delivery is at the seller's premises, the seller is responsible for loading. The risk passes when the goods are loaded onto the buyer's carrier. If delivery is at another place, the risk passes when the goods are delivered to the carrier's vehicle without loading. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a risk category listed in the ITF course material?
opts: A. Currency risk
B. Sovereign risk
C. Transfer risk
D. Documentation risk
questionBank.exp: The course lists Payment, Performance, Political/Country, Transaction, Non-Acceptance, Transfer, Sovereign, Documentation, and Legal risks. Currency risk is not listed as a separate category; it is considered part of foreign exchange exposure rather than a distinct trade risk. (Module 1.1)

questionBank.q: A bank has issued a Letter of Credit for an importer. The importer is a new customer with no credit history. Which risk to the issuing bank is most prominent?
opts: A. Credit risk of the applicant
B. Documentation risk
C. Performance risk of the seller
D. Country risk
questionBank.exp: The issuing bank faces the risk that the applicant may not be in a position to pay when the documents are presented. This is the applicant's credit risk, which is a primary consideration when issuing an L/C. (Module 1.2, but also covered under issuing bank risks in Module 3)

questionBank.q: A buyer has agreed to pay for goods under a Collection (D/P) arrangement. The buyer refuses to pay when the documents are presented because the goods have not yet arrived. Which party bears the risk of this refusal?
opts: A. The buyer
B. The seller
C. The remitting bank
D. The collecting bank
questionBank.exp: Under a D/P collection, the buyer is not obligated to pay until they accept the documents. If the buyer refuses, the seller must bear the consequences (e.g., storage, return shipping, or loss of sale). This is a key risk for the seller in collections. (Module 1.2, and Module 4)

questionBank.q: A seller ships goods under a documentary collection with instructions 'Deliver documents against acceptance' (D/A). The buyer accepts the bill of exchange but later defaults on payment. Which party bears the ultimate risk of non-payment?
opts: A. The buyer
B. The seller
C. The collecting bank, because they accepted the bill
D. The remitting bank, because they forwarded the documents
questionBank.exp: Under a D/A collection, the seller retains the risk that the buyer will default on payment even after accepting the bill. The banks are not guarantors of payment; they only act as intermediaries. This is a fundamental risk of collections. (Module 1.2, and Module 4)

questionBank.q: Which payment method offers the lowest risk to the exporter but the highest risk to the importer?
opts: A. Advance Payment
B. Open Account
C. Collection
D. Documentary Credit
questionBank.exp: With Advance Payment, the exporter receives payment before shipping, eliminating their risk. The importer bears all risk (the seller may not ship, may ship wrong goods, etc.). This is why Advance Payment is at the top of the trust league table from the seller's perspective. (Module 1.2)

questionBank.q: A seller in the UK and a buyer in the USA have a contract for goods under CIF New York. The seller has obtained insurance under Institute Cargo Clause C. Is this sufficient?
opts: A. Yes, CIF requires minimum cover under Clause C
B. No, CIF requires all-risk cover under Clause A
C. No, CIF requires no insurance
D. Yes, but only if the buyer agrees
questionBank.exp: Under Incoterms 2020, CIF still requires only minimum cover (Institute Cargo Clause C). This is a key distinction from CIP which now requires Clause A. The seller's obligation under CIF is to obtain insurance at the minimum level, unless otherwise agreed. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A seller in South Africa agrees to ship goods to a buyer in China under DAP. The seller arranges carriage to the buyer's warehouse in Shanghai. The truck arrives, but the buyer does not have space to unload immediately. The truck incurs waiting charges. Who pays the waiting charges?
opts: A. The seller, because risk has not yet passed
B. The buyer, because risk passed when the goods arrived at the named place
C. The carrier, because they should have anticipated the delay
D. Shared equally
questionBank.exp: Under DAP, risk passes when the goods are placed at the disposal of the buyer on the arriving means of transport. After that point, the buyer bears all costs, including waiting charges, as they are responsible for unloading. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: An exporter in France ships goods to a buyer in Canada under FOB Le Havre. The buyer has arranged the vessel. The goods are loaded, but the Bill of Lading shows 'Shipper's load and count'. What does this notation mean for the carrier's liability?
opts: A. The carrier is not responsible for verifying the quantity or quality of goods
B. The carrier confirms the quantity and quality
C. The carrier assumes full liability for the goods
D. The notation is invalid under FOB
questionBank.exp: A Bill of Lading marked 'Shipper's load and count' or 'Said to Contain' indicates the carrier could not verify the quantity or quality of the goods. This is common in FOB shipments where the seller loads the containers and the carrier accepts the container as is. (Module 1.2, also in the Bill of Lading section)

questionBank.q: A buyer in the EU purchases goods from a seller in Brazil under CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid To). The seller must obtain insurance covering Institute Cargo Clause A. If the seller only obtains Clause C, what is the consequence?
opts: A. The seller is in breach of Incoterms 2020 and must bear any losses not covered
B. The buyer must accept it because insurance is for the buyer's benefit
C. The seller is allowed to choose Clause C as a minimum
D. The carrier will automatically provide the correct cover
questionBank.exp: Under Incoterms 2020, CIP requires all-risk cover (Clause A). If the seller only obtains Clause C, the seller has not complied with the contract and would be liable for any losses that would have been covered under Clause A. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A seller in the UAE agrees to sell to a buyer in India under FCA (Free Carrier) at a named place other than the seller's premises. The seller delivers the goods to the carrier's vehicle at that place. Who is responsible for loading the goods onto the carrier's vehicle?
opts: A. The seller, because FCA always requires seller to load
B. The buyer, because FCA at a named place requires the buyer to load
C. The carrier, because they provide the vehicle
D. The seller and buyer jointly
questionBank.exp: Under FCA, if delivery is at a named place other than the seller's premises, the seller must deliver the goods to the carrier's vehicle without loading it. The buyer is responsible for loading at that point. This is a nuance of FCA. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A contract states EXW (seller's factory). The buyer arranges for a truck to collect the goods. The seller refuses to assist with loading, citing EXW terms. The buyer claims that under EXW the seller must at least help. Who is correct?
opts: A. The seller, because EXW does not require the seller to load
B. The buyer, because the seller must assist with loading if asked
C. The seller, but only if the goods are not dangerous
D. The carrier, because they must load
questionBank.exp: Under EXW, the seller's obligation is minimal: they place the goods at the disposal of the buyer. The seller does not need to load the goods on any collecting vehicle, nor clear them for export. The buyer is entirely responsible. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A seller in Norway ships goods to a buyer in Chile under CFR. The goods are damaged during unloading at the destination port. Which party should claim against the carrier (if any)?
opts: A. The seller, because CFR requires the seller to arrange carriage
B. The buyer, because the risk passed once the goods were on board the vessel
C. The carrier, because they are always liable
D. The bank, because they hold the documents
questionBank.exp: Under CFR, the risk of loss passes when the goods are on board the vessel. Any damage during unloading is a risk borne by the buyer, who would have a claim against the carrier if the carrier was negligent. The seller is not responsible. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A buyer in the UK has agreed to pay under a Documentary Credit. The seller presents documents that conform. The issuing bank is located in a country with a sovereign debt default. The confirming bank (in the UK) has already paid the seller. The issuing bank cannot reimburse the confirming bank. Which party bears the loss?
opts: A. The seller, because they should have checked the issuing bank
B. The confirming bank, because they assumed the risk
C. The buyer, because they are ultimately responsible
D. The confirming bank can recover from the buyer
questionBank.exp: The confirming bank substitutes its own creditworthiness for that of the issuing bank. If the issuing bank defaults, the confirming bank bears the loss. This is a key risk for confirming banks. (Module 1.2, but also covered under confirming bank risks in Module 3)

questionBank.q: An exporter ships goods under a Letter of Credit that specifies 'partial shipments not allowed'. The exporter ships 80% of the goods and presents documents for that amount. The issuing bank:
opts: A. Must pay for the partial shipment because it is a valid drawdown
B. Must reject the documents because partial shipment is prohibited
C. Must accept the documents if the buyer agrees
D. Must pay the full amount to maintain the L/C
questionBank.exp: If the L/C prohibits partial shipments, any shipment of less than the full quantity is a discrepancy. The bank must reject the presentation because it does not comply with the terms. (Module 1.2, also in Module 3)

questionBank.q: A seller in Indonesia and a buyer in the Philippines agree on FOB Jakarta. The seller loads the goods on board the vessel. The Bill of Lading is issued but is marked 'Received for shipment' rather than 'On Board'. The buyer's L/C requires an 'On Board' Bill of Lading. What should the seller do?
opts: A. Present the 'Received for shipment' B/L as it is still valid
B. Request the carrier to add an 'On Board' notation
C. Ask the buyer to amend the L/C
D. Ship again with a new Bill of Lading
questionBank.exp: Under a L/C that requires 'On Board' notation, a 'Received for shipment' Bill of Lading is not acceptable. The seller should request the carrier to add an 'On Board' notation to the Bill of Lading, which is a common practice. (Module 1.2, and transport document requirements)

questionBank.q: A buyer in South Africa imports goods from a seller in Germany under CIF Durban. The seller obtains insurance with Institute Cargo Clause C. During the voyage, the goods are damaged due to improper stowage by the carrier. Which insurance cover would respond to this loss?
opts: A. Clause C covers this, so the buyer can claim
B. Clause C would not cover improper stowage, so the buyer cannot claim from the seller's policy
C. The buyer can claim from the carrier directly
D. The seller must reimburse the buyer because the seller chose Clause C
questionBank.exp: Institute Cargo Clause C provides minimum cover, typically excluding improper stowage (as that is a carrier's liability). The buyer's remedy would be against the carrier for negligence in stowage, not the insurance policy. (Module 1.3, but requires understanding of insurance cover)

questionBank.q: A seller in Australia and a buyer in New Zealand agree on DAP Auckland. The seller arranges for the goods to be delivered to the buyer's warehouse. The goods are stolen from the truck while parked at the buyer's warehouse before unloading. Who bears the loss?
opts: A. The seller, because the goods had not been unloaded
B. The buyer, because the goods were placed at the buyer's disposal on the truck
C. The carrier, because the theft occurred during transit
D. The police, because theft is a criminal matter
questionBank.exp: Under DAP, the risk passes when the goods are placed at the disposal of the buyer on the arriving means of transport. Since the truck was at the buyer's warehouse, risk had passed to the buyer, who bears the loss. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A buyer in the USA and a seller in Mexico agree on FAS at a US port. The seller places the goods alongside the vessel at the port. Before the vessel arrives, a fire at the port damages the goods. Which party bears the loss?
opts: A. The seller, because risk passes only when the vessel is alongside and ready to load
B. The buyer, because risk passed when the goods were placed alongside the vessel
C. The carrier, because the vessel was not yet there
D. The port authority, because the fire was on their premises
questionBank.exp: Under FAS, risk passes when the goods are placed alongside the vessel (on the quay or barge), regardless of whether the vessel is actually present. Therefore, the buyer bears the loss from that moment. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A seller in Singapore sells to a buyer in Malaysia under EXW. The buyer sends a truck to pick up the goods. The goods are loaded by the buyer's driver. While driving to the border, the truck is involved in an accident and the goods are damaged. Who bears the loss?
opts: A. The seller, because EXW means the seller is responsible until the border
B. The buyer, because risk passed when the goods were loaded and left the premises
C. The carrier, because the driver was their employee
D. Shared between buyer and seller
questionBank.exp: Under EXW, risk passes when the goods are placed at the buyer's disposal at the seller's premises. Once the buyer's driver loads and leaves, the buyer bears all risks. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A contract for the sale of goods includes the term 'FOB Shanghai'. The seller has arranged for the goods to be loaded on board a vessel named 'Star'. The Bill of Lading shows the vessel name and 'On Board' notation. The buyer's bank requires a 'Clean' Bill of Lading. The carrier notes on the Bill of Lading 'one carton damaged'. Is this a Clean Bill of Lading?
opts: A. Yes, because 'On Board' is what matters
B. No, because any notation of damage makes it 'Claused' or 'Foul'
C. Yes, but only if the damage is minor
D. No, because the carrier must always indicate damage
questionBank.exp: A Clean Bill of Lading is one that does not contain any adverse notations about the condition of the goods or packaging. A notation of damage makes it a 'Claused' or 'Foul' Bill of Lading, which banks will usually reject under a L/C. (Module 1.2, Bill of Lading quality)

questionBank.q: A seller in the UK ships goods to a buyer in Australia under CFR. The buyer has arranged for marine insurance separately. The goods are lost at sea. The buyer claims on their own insurance policy, but the insurer disputes that the buyer had an insurable interest at the time of loss. Under CFR, did the buyer have an insurable interest?
opts: A. No, because the risk was with the seller until arrival
B. Yes, because under CFR the risk passes on board, so the buyer had an interest
C. Yes, but only if the seller had paid the freight
D. No, because the buyer had not paid for the goods
questionBank.exp: Under CFR, risk passes when the goods are on board the vessel. From that point, the buyer bears the risk of loss and therefore has an insurable interest. The buyer can claim under their own insurance. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A seller in Chile and a buyer in Japan agree on DDP. The seller must clear the goods for import into Japan. The seller appoints a customs broker in Japan. The broker makes an error in the customs declaration, leading to a fine. Who bears the fine?
opts: A. The buyer, because the broker was the buyer's agent
B. The seller, because DDP makes the seller responsible for import clearance
C. The broker, because they made the error
D. Shared between seller and buyer
questionBank.exp: Under DDP, the seller is responsible for all import formalities and bears all costs and risks associated with import clearance. If the seller's agent (the broker) makes an error, the seller bears the financial consequences. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: An importer in Nigeria has agreed to pay under a Documentary Credit. The issuing bank has received conforming documents and is about to pay. The importer instructs the bank to refuse payment because the goods have not arrived and the importer suspects fraud. Which party is legally required to pay?
opts: A. The importer, because the L/C is a separate contract from the sale
B. The issuing bank, because it must honor conforming documents
C. The importer can refuse, so the bank must not pay
D. The confirming bank, if any, must pay the seller
questionBank.exp: Under UCP, banks deal in documents only. If the documents comply with the L/C terms, the issuing bank must pay, regardless of the status of the goods. The buyer cannot stop payment based on goods issues. The L/C is a separate contract from the sales contract. (Module 1.2, and also UCP article 4)

questionBank.q: A seller in the USA ships to a buyer in Brazil under FCA (Free Carrier). The seller delivers the goods to the carrier at a terminal. The carrier issues a Bill of Lading but does not indicate the port of loading clearly. The buyer's bank refuses the documents under the L/C. Who is responsible for ensuring the Bill of Lading has the correct port?
opts: A. The seller, because they are responsible for the documents
B. The buyer, because they arranged the carrier
C. The carrier, because they issued the document
D. The bank, because they must interpret the L/C
questionBank.exp: Under FCA, the seller is responsible for delivering the goods and providing the transport document that meets the L/C requirements. The seller should check that the Bill of Lading correctly states the port of loading as specified in the L/C. (Module 1.2, and also buyer's responsibility under L/C)

questionBank.q: A buyer in Europe and a seller in China agree on CIP (Carriage and Insurance Paid To) to a named place in France. The seller has obtained insurance under Institute Cargo Clause A. The goods are lost at sea. The buyer files a claim with the insurer. The insurer pays the claim. Who paid for the insurance premium?
opts: A. The seller, because CIP requires the seller to pay for insurance
B. The buyer, because they bear the risk
C. The carrier, because they are responsible for transport
D. The bank, because it is part of the L/C
questionBank.exp: Under CIP, the seller must contract for insurance and pay the premium. Although the insurance is for the buyer's benefit, the seller bears the cost of procuring it. (Module 1.3)

questionBank.q: A bank receives a Bill of Lading that is consigned 'to order of XYZ Bank'. The exporter has endorsed the Bill of Lading on the back. Which type of Bill of Lading is this?
opts: A. Straight Bill of Lading
B. Order Bill of Lading
C. Received for Shipment Bill of Lading
D. Clean Bill of Lading
questionBank.exp: An Order Bill of Lading is consigned to the order of a specified party and can be transferred by endorsement. The bank can endorse it to the importer upon payment. This is the negotiable type used as collateral. (Module 2.2)

questionBank.q: An importer's bank has received a Bill of Lading that is consigned directly to the importer's name, with no endorsement space. The bank cannot transfer title to another party using this document. This is a:
opts: A. Order Bill of Lading
B. Straight Bill of Lading
C. Clean Bill of Lading
D. Through Bill of Lading
questionBank.exp: A Straight Bill of Lading is consigned to a specified party and cannot be transferred by endorsement. Banks typically avoid these for financing because they cannot control title. (Module 2.2)

questionBank.q: A carrier issues a Bill of Lading that states 'Shipper's load and count' and makes no mention of the condition of the goods inside the container. What does this notation indicate about the carrier's acceptance?
opts: A. The carrier confirms the goods are in good condition
B. The carrier could not verify the quantity or quality and therefore assumes no liability
C. The carrier is fully liable for the contents
D. The carrier has inspected and approved the goods
questionBank.exp: A notation like 'Shipper's load and count' means the carrier is unable to verify the quantity or quality of the goods inside the container. It is a disclaimer of liability for internal condition. (Module 2.2)

questionBank.q: A bank is examining a Bill of Lading that has no adverse notations about the goods or packaging. The Bill of Lading is marked 'Clean on board'. Which function of the Bill of Lading does this notation primarily serve?
opts: A. It serves as a receipt for the goods
B. It serves as evidence of the contract of carriage
C. It serves as a document of title
D. It serves as an insurance document
questionBank.exp: The cleanliness notation (clean vs. claused) relates to the Bill of Lading's function as a receipt for the goods. A clean Bill of Lading states the goods were received in apparent good order and condition. (Module 2.2)

questionBank.q: A seller presents a Bill of Lading that shows 'one carton crushed' on the face. The Letter of Credit requires a 'Clean Bill of Lading'. The bank should:
opts: A. Accept it because the notation is minor
B. Reject it because it is a claused/foul Bill of Lading
C. Accept it if the buyer agrees
D. Request an amendment to the L/C
questionBank.exp: Any notation of damage or defect makes the Bill of Lading 'claused' or 'foul'. A Letter of Credit requiring a clean Bill of Lading would not accept this. The bank must reject as a discrepancy. (Module 2.2)

questionBank.q: A bank is financing an import transaction and requires security over the goods in transit. Which type of Bill of Lading would give the bank the best control over the goods?
opts: A. Straight Bill of Lading
B. Order Bill of Lading consigned to the bank's order
C. Air Waybill
D. Sea Waybill
questionBank.exp: An Order Bill of Lading consigned to the bank's order allows the bank to maintain title and control until the importer pays. It is negotiable and can be endorsed to release goods. This is why banks prefer it as collateral. (Module 2.2)

questionBank.q: A carrier issues a Bill of Lading that states 'Received for shipment' but does not yet show an 'On Board' date. The L/C requires an 'On Board' Bill of Lading. The seller can:
opts: A. Present it as is, because 'Received for shipment' is acceptable
B. Request the carrier to add an 'On Board' notation after loading
C. Ask the buyer to amend the L/C
D. Re-ship the goods
questionBank.exp: A 'Received for shipment' Bill of Lading can be converted to an 'On Board' Bill of Lading by the carrier adding an 'On Board' notation with the date of loading. This is a common practice. (Module 2.2)

questionBank.q: A seller has shipped goods and the Bill of Lading is consigned 'to order of the shipper'. The seller endorses the Bill of Lading in blank. What does this allow?
opts: A. Only the seller can take delivery
B. The Bill of Lading becomes a bearer document that anyone holding it can take delivery
C. The buyer must endorse it again
D. The carrier must reissue the Bill of Lading
questionBank.exp: When the shipper endorses a Bill of Lading in blank (without naming a specific endorsee), it becomes a bearer document. Anyone presenting the original can claim the goods. This is a negotiable instrument. (Module 2.2)

questionBank.q: A buyer under an L/C has received documents including a Bill of Lading that is 'Straight' consigned to the buyer. The buyer's bank notices the L/C required the Bill of Lading to be 'to the order of the issuing bank'. The bank should:
opts: A. Accept it because the buyer is the consignee
B. Reject it as a discrepancy
C. Accept it because the bank can still control
D. Return it to the seller for amendment
questionBank.exp: The L/C requirement for an Order Bill of Lading (to the order of the issuing bank) is a condition. A Straight Bill of Lading does not comply because it is non-negotiable and the bank cannot control title. This is a discrepancy. (Module 2.2)

questionBank.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of a Bill of Lading as described in the course material?
opts: A. A receipt issued by the carrier
B. Evidence of a shipping contract
C. A document of title to the goods
D. A guarantee of the quality of goods
questionBank.exp: The three functions are: (1) receipt for goods, (2) evidence of contract of carriage, (3) document of title. It does not guarantee quality; that is a commercial issue. (Module 2.2)

questionBank.q: A Bill of Exchange is defined as an unconditional order in writing addressed by one party to another, signed by the drawer, requiring the drawee to pay a certain sum of money to a specified party. Which element makes it 'unconditional'?
opts: A. It must be payable at a fixed or determinable future time
B. It cannot be subject to any conditions or contingencies
C. It must be accepted by the drawee
D. It must be in a set of two originals
questionBank.exp: The order must be unconditional — payment cannot be subject to any condition. This is a fundamental requirement for a valid Bill of Exchange. (Module 2.3)

questionBank.q: A seller draws a Bill of Exchange on the buyer for USD 100,000 at 60 days sight. The buyer accepts the bill by signing 'ACCEPTED' and dating it. This creates a:
opts: A. Banker's Acceptance
B. Trade Acceptance
C. Promissory Note
D. Sight Draft
questionBank.exp: A Trade Acceptance is a Bill of Exchange drawn on and accepted by an individual or corporate (the buyer). A Banker's Acceptance would be drawn on and accepted by a bank. (Module 2.3)

questionBank.q: Which of the following best distinguishes a Banker's Acceptance from a Trade Acceptance?
opts: A. A Banker's Acceptance is drawn on a bank and has lower credit risk
B. A Trade Acceptance is always payable at sight
C. A Banker's Acceptance cannot be discounted
D. A Trade Acceptance is negotiable, a Banker's Acceptance is not
questionBank.exp: A Banker's Acceptance carries the credit of a bank, making it lower risk and more readily discountable at a cheaper rate than a Trade Acceptance (which depends on the credit of a corporate buyer). (Module 2.3)

questionBank.q: A bank has accepted a Bill of Exchange drawn by an exporter on the bank under a Letter of Credit. The bill is now a Banker's Acceptance. The exporter wishes to sell the bill before maturity to obtain cash. This is called:
opts: A. Discounting
B. Factoring
C. Forfaiting
D. Avalization
questionBank.exp: Discounting is the sale of an accepted Bill of Exchange before its maturity at a discount from face value. Banker's Acceptances are particularly marketable and can be discounted easily. (Module 2.3, and Module 5)

questionBank.q: A seller in Germany ships goods to a buyer in France under a Collection (D/A). The seller draws a Bill of Exchange at 90 days from Bill of Lading date. The buyer accepts the bill. The seller's bank now holds an accepted bill. What is the key risk for the seller at this point?
opts: A. The buyer may not accept the bill
B. The buyer may default at maturity
C. The carrier may not deliver the goods
D. The bank may lose the bill
questionBank.exp: The seller has already shipped goods. The buyer accepted the bill, but acceptance does not guarantee payment at maturity. The seller still bears the payment risk — this is a key risk in collections. (Module 2.3)

questionBank.q: A Bill of Exchange is drawn by a creditor on a debtor. In contrast, a Promissory Note is:
opts: A. Drawn by the creditor on the debtor
B. Drawn by the debtor on the creditor
C. An order to pay
D. Issued by a bank only
questionBank.exp: A Promissory Note is a promise by the maker (debtor) to pay the payee (creditor). In a Bill of Exchange, the drawer is the creditor, and the drawee is the debtor. This is a key distinction. (Module 2.3, comparison table)

questionBank.q: Which of the following is true regarding the number of parties in a Bill of Exchange versus a Promissory Note?
opts: A. A Bill of Exchange has two parties, a Promissory Note has three
B. A Bill of Exchange has three parties, a Promissory Note has two
C. Both have three parties
D. Both have two parties
questionBank.exp: A Bill of Exchange has three parties: Drawer, Drawee, and Payee. A Promissory Note has two: Maker and Payee. (Module 2.3, comparison table)

questionBank.q: In a Bill of Exchange, the drawer's liability is secondary, meaning:
opts: A. The drawer is primarily liable and must pay first
B. The drawer's liability arises only if the drawee fails to pay
C. The drawer is not liable at all
D. The drawer is liable only if the bill is not accepted
questionBank.exp: Under a Bill of Exchange, the drawee (or acceptor) is primarily liable. The drawer's liability is secondary and only arises if the drawee defaults. In a Promissory Note, the maker's liability is primary. (Module 2.3, comparison table)

questionBank.q: A seller has drawn a Bill of Exchange on the buyer for USD 50,000. The buyer accepts the bill and returns it to the seller. The seller then presents the accepted bill to a bank for discounting. The bank will typically discount at a rate that reflects:
opts: A. The credit risk of the seller
B. The credit risk of the buyer (or the acceptor)
C. The country risk of the seller's country
D. The freight cost
questionBank.exp: The discount rate on a Trade Acceptance is based on the creditworthiness of the acceptor (the buyer). If the acceptor is a bank (Banker's Acceptance), the rate is lower. (Module 2.3, and Module 5A)

questionBank.q: A Bill of Exchange must state a determinable future time for payment. Which of the following is an acceptable expression of a determinable future time?
opts: A. 30 days after Bill of Lading date
B. As soon as goods arrive
C. When the buyer sells the goods
D. Upon request
questionBank.exp: A determinable future time must be fixed or readily calculable, such as a specific number of days from a specific event (Bill of Lading date). 'As soon as goods arrive' or 'when sold' are not determinable. (Module 2.3)

questionBank.q: A bank receives a Bill of Exchange that has been accepted by the buyer. The bank wants to use this bill as collateral for a loan to the seller. Which feature makes this bill a marketable instrument?
opts: A. It is drawn in a set of two originals
B. It is a negotiable instrument that can be transferred by endorsement
C. It is payable to a specific party only
D. It must be presented for payment within 30 days
questionBank.exp: Bills of Exchange are negotiable instruments and can be transferred by endorsement, making them marketable. This is why banks can discount them or use them as collateral. (Module 2.3)

questionBank.q: An exporter has received a Letter of Credit that requires '2/3 original Bills of Lading' among the documents. What does this requirement mean?
opts: A. The exporter must present two of the three originals
B. The exporter must present both originals and three copies
C. The exporter must present three originals
D. The exporter must present one original and two copies
questionBank.exp: Bills of Lading are typically issued in sets of three originals. A requirement for '2/3' means the exporter must present two of the three original copies. The remaining original may be sent separately or retained. (Module 2.2, as seen in sample L/Cs)

questionBank.q: A bank is reviewing a Commercial Invoice submitted under a Letter of Credit. The invoice describes the goods as 'Caramel 3240 H.S. Jumbo' but the L/C describes 'Caramel 3240 H.S. Jumbo - details as per proforma invoice'. The invoice also references the proforma invoice. The bank should:
opts: A. Reject because the invoice description does not match exactly
B. Accept if the invoice description is not contradictory
C. Reject because the L/C did not allow reference to proforma
D. Request a correction from the seller
questionBank.exp: Under UCP, a Commercial Invoice must not describe goods in a manner that is contradictory to the L/C. If the L/C provides a general description with reference to a proforma, the invoice can describe goods in more detail, as long as it does not conflict. (Module 2.2, and UCP Article 18)

questionBank.q: Which document is typically issued as proof that the goods have been inspected and meet the quality standards specified in the contract?
opts: A. Commercial Invoice
B. Packing List
C. Certificate of Analysis
D. Bill of Lading
questionBank.exp: A Certificate of Analysis is a regulatory document that confirms the goods meet specified quality or composition standards. This is often required for chemicals, food products, etc. (Module 2.1, Regulatory Documents)

questionBank.q: A buyer in Nigeria has imported goods and requires a Combined Certificate of Value and Origin (CCVO) on Form C.16. This document serves which purposes?
opts: A. It combines commercial invoice and certificate of origin functions
B. It serves only as a certificate of value for customs
C. It is used only for insurance claims
D. It replaces the Bill of Lading
questionBank.exp: The CCVO on Form C.16 is a regulatory document that combines a declaration of the value of goods and their country of origin, used for customs purposes in Nigeria. It is a commercial/regulatory hybrid. (Module 2.1, and sample L/Cs)

questionBank.q: An exporter submits a Bill of Lading that is 'Claused' with a notation that the goods were received in damaged packaging. The Letter of Credit requires a 'Clean' Bill of Lading. Which of the following options is available to the exporter?
opts: A. Present the claused Bill of Lading and hope the bank overlooks it
B. Ask the carrier to issue a clean Bill of Lading despite the damage
C. Correct the discrepancy by obtaining a new clean Bill of Lading if possible, or seek a waiver
D. Amend the L/C to accept a claused Bill of Lading
questionBank.exp: The exporter can attempt to correct the discrepancy by obtaining a new Bill of Lading if the carrier agrees to remove the notation (unlikely if damage is real). Otherwise, the exporter must seek a waiver from the buyer or present on a collection basis. (Module 3.10, rejected documents options)

questionBank.q: A bank has received a Bill of Exchange that is not properly endorsed. The bank refuses to honour the presentation. The seller claims the bank should accept because the draft is valid. Which party is correct?
opts: A. The seller, because the bill is a valid order
B. The bank, because proper endorsement is required for negotiation
C. The buyer, because they must accept regardless
D. The carrier, because they hold the goods
questionBank.exp: For a Bill of Exchange to be negotiable, it must be properly endorsed. If the bill is payable to order and not endorsed, the bank cannot negotiate it. The bank is correct to refuse. (Module 2.3, and list of discrepancies)

questionBank.q: A seller under a Deferred Payment L/C does not wish to draw a Bill of Exchange to avoid stamp duty. The bank instead issues a document stating that payment will be made on a specified future date. This document is called a:
opts: A. Banker's Acceptance
B. Deferred Payment Undertaking
C. Promissory Note
D. Aval
questionBank.exp: In some countries, drawing a Bill of Exchange incurs stamp duty. To avoid this, the seller may request the bank to issue a Deferred Payment Undertaking, which is a promise to pay on the maturity date without a bill. (Module 3.4, Deferred Payment L/C, though this is in the L/C section, it's part of Bill of Exchange dynamics)

questionBank.q: A buyer in the UK purchases goods from a seller in India. The contract is on Open Account terms. The seller ships the goods and sends a Commercial Invoice. The invoice shows 'terms: net 30 days'. This means:
opts: A. The buyer must pay within 30 days of invoice date
B. The buyer must pay 30 days after receipt of goods
C. The buyer must pay 30 days after Bill of Lading date
D. The buyer has 30 days to inspect goods
questionBank.exp: Net 30 days typically means payment is due 30 days from the invoice date, unless otherwise specified. This is a standard open account term. (Module 1.2, though Open Account not in Module 2, but it's implied)

questionBank.q: A bank is examining a set of shipping documents. The Bill of Lading shows the port of loading as 'Hamburg' but the Letter of Credit specifies 'Any EEC seaport'. The bank should:
opts: A. Reject because Hamburg is not specifically listed
B. Accept because Hamburg is an EEC seaport
C. Reject because the port must be exactly as in the L/C
D. Accept only if the carrier confirms
questionBank.exp: If the L/C allows 'Any EEC seaport', any port within the European Economic Community is acceptable. Hamburg qualifies. The bank should accept. (This is from sample L/Cs, illustrating interpretation of L/C terms)

questionBank.q: A seller presents documents under a Letter of Credit. The Commercial Invoice has a total of USD 50,000, but the Bill of Lading shows freight prepaid of USD 2,000. The L/C value is USD 50,000 CFR. Should the bank treat this as a discrepancy?
opts: A. Yes, because the invoice includes freight, making total over L/C value
B. No, because CFR includes freight in the price, and the invoice total is consistent
C. Yes, because freight must be shown separately
D. No, because the Bill of Lading is a transport document, not a commercial document
questionBank.exp: Under CFR, the price includes freight. The invoice total of USD 50,000 is the CFR value. The fact that the Bill of Lading shows freight paid separately is not a discrepancy; it merely confirms the seller has paid freight. The documents are consistent. (Module 2.2, and Incoterms understanding)

questionBank.q: A Banker's Acceptance is typically more marketable and discounts at a lower rate than a Trade Acceptance. This is because:
opts: A. Banker's Acceptances are always at sight
B. Banker's Acceptances are issued by a bank, which has lower credit risk
C. Trade Acceptances cannot be discounted
D. Banker's Acceptances are guaranteed by the government
questionBank.exp: The lower risk associated with a bank's credit (compared to a corporate buyer's credit) makes Banker's Acceptances more attractive to investors, leading to lower discount rates. (Module 2.3)

questionBank.q: A seller has received a Letter of Credit that requires a 'Manufacturer's Certificate of Production stating standards adopted'. This document is an example of:
opts: A. Commercial document
B. Financial document
C. Regulatory document
D. Transport document
questionBank.exp: A Manufacturer's Certificate of Production is a regulatory document that certifies the goods were produced according to certain standards, often required for customs or quality compliance. (Module 2.1, Regulatory Documents)

questionBank.q: A bank has received a Bill of Lading that is endorsed to the order of the bank. The bank releases the Bill of Lading to the importer against payment. The importer then uses the Bill of Lading to clear the goods. This process demonstrates the Bill of Lading's function as:
opts: A. A receipt
B. A contract of carriage
C. A document of title
D. An insurance document
questionBank.exp: The ability to transfer title by endorsement and delivery, and to use the document to claim the goods, is the essence of the document of title function. (Module 2.2)

questionBank.q: A Bill of Exchange is drawn 'at sight'. The drawee must pay:
opts: A. Upon presentation
B. 30 days after acceptance
C. At a fixed future date
D. When the goods arrive
questionBank.exp: A sight bill is payable on demand upon presentation. 'At sight' means payment is due immediately upon presentation of the bill. (Module 2.3)

questionBank.q: A seller in Italy ships goods to a buyer in the USA. The seller draws a Bill of Exchange on the buyer at 60 days from Bill of Lading date. The buyer accepts the bill. The bill is now a:
opts: A. Sight draft
B. Trade Acceptance
C. Banker's Acceptance
D. Deferred Payment Undertaking
questionBank.exp: Since the bill is drawn on and accepted by the buyer (a corporate), it is a Trade Acceptance. A Banker's Acceptance would require a bank as drawee/acceptor. (Module 2.3)

questionBank.q: A bank is reviewing a Commercial Invoice that describes the goods as 'Agricultural processing equipment' but the L/C describes 'New agricultural processing equipment'. The invoice description is:
opts: A. Acceptable because it is not contradictory
B. A discrepancy because 'new' is missing
C. Acceptable because the L/C description is generic
D. A discrepancy because the invoice is not detailed enough
questionBank.exp: Under UCP, the Commercial Invoice must not describe goods in a contradictory manner. Adding 'new' is a material difference; if the L/C requires 'new', the invoice must state 'new' or at least not contradict. Missing it may be a discrepancy. (Module 2.2, and UCP Article 18)

questionBank.q: A seller presents a Bill of Lading that is 'Received for shipment' and has an 'On Board' notation added later with the date '10 Jan'. The Bill of Lading also shows a pre-printed date '5 Jan'. Which date is the shipment date for purposes of the L/C?
opts: A. 5 Jan (the pre-printed date)
B. 10 Jan (the On Board notation date)
C. Both dates are acceptable
D. The later of the two
questionBank.exp: When an 'On Board' notation is added to a 'Received for shipment' Bill of Lading, the date of the notation is deemed the date of shipment. This is a standard UCP rule. (Module 2.2, and UCP Article 20)

questionBank.q: A bank has received a Bill of Exchange that is not signed by the drawer. The bank should:
opts: A. Accept it because signatures are not required
B. Reject it because a Bill of Exchange must be signed by the drawer
C. Ask the beneficiary to sign it
D. Accept it and request the buyer to sign
questionBank.exp: A Bill of Exchange must be signed by the party giving it (the drawer). An unsigned bill is invalid and would be rejected as a discrepancy. (Module 2.3)

questionBank.q: A seller under a Letter of Credit presents a Commercial Invoice that is addressed to the applicant, but the L/C requires the invoice to be made out in the name of the issuing bank. The bank should:
opts: A. Accept it because the applicant is the buyer
B. Reject it because the invoice is incorrectly addressed
C. Accept it if the applicant agrees
D. Return it to the seller for correction
questionBank.exp: If the L/C specifies who the invoice should be addressed to, the invoice must comply. Addressing it to the applicant instead of the issuing bank is a discrepancy. (Module 2.2, and sample discrepancies list)

questionBank.q: A Clean Report of Inspection (CRI) is typically required for imports into certain countries. This document is issued by:
opts: A. The carrier
B. A pre-shipment inspection company
C. The seller's bank
D. The buyer's customs
questionBank.exp: A Clean Report of Inspection (CRI) is issued by a pre-shipment inspection company appointed by the importing country to verify quality, quantity, and price before shipment. It is a regulatory document. (Module 2.1, Regulatory Documents)

questionBank.q: A seller has shipped goods under a Letter of Credit. The Bill of Lading is dated 15 March, but the shipment was actually loaded on 14 March. The carrier backdates the Bill of Lading to 14 March. This is a practice known as:
opts: A. Antedating
B. Post-dating
C. Stale Bill of Lading
D. Forged Bill of Lading
questionBank.exp: Antedating is the practice of dating a Bill of Lading earlier than the actual loading date. This is generally not permitted and could constitute fraud. Banks rely on the Bill of Lading date as presented. (Module 2.2, though not explicitly named, it's a known issue)

questionBank.q: A bank is examining a Bill of Lading that shows the goods were 'shipped on board' but the Bill of Lading is not signed by the carrier or its agent. The bank should:
opts: A. Accept it because the 'shipped on board' notation is sufficient
B. Reject it because the Bill of Lading must be signed
C. Accept it if the carrier is identifiable
D. Request a correction
questionBank.exp: A Bill of Lading must be signed by the carrier or its agent to be valid. Without a signature, it is not a valid transport document and would be rejected. (Module 2.2, and UCP Article 20)

questionBank.q: A seller presents a set of documents under a collection. The Commercial Invoice shows the Incoterm as 'CIF Lagos', but the Bill of Lading shows 'Freight Prepaid' and there is no insurance document. The collection instruction does not require insurance. The bank:
opts: A. Must reject because CIF requires insurance
B. Must accept if the collection order does not require insurance
C. Must ask the seller to provide insurance
D. Must return documents
questionBank.exp: In a collection, the bank acts on the instructions of the collection order. If the collection order does not require insurance, the bank is not obligated to check for it. The seller's contract may require it, but the bank is not responsible for enforcing contract terms beyond the collection instructions. (Module 4, but this tests document understanding in a collection context)

questionBank.q: A seller receives a Letter of Credit that requires a 'Cargo Tracking Note'. The seller has never heard of this document. The seller should:
opts: A. Ignore it and ship anyway
B. Contact the buyer or issuing bank to clarify the requirement
C. Provide a substitute document
D. Ask the carrier to issue one
questionBank.exp: If a required document is unfamiliar, the seller should seek clarification from the buyer or issuing bank to understand what is expected. The seller cannot assume a substitute is acceptable. This is a practical advice. (Module 2.2, and practical L/C handling)

questionBank.q: An exporter in Europe receives a Letter of Credit for EUR 100,000. The exporter is actually a middleman who sources goods from a manufacturer in Asia. The exporter wants to transfer EUR 75,000 of the L/C to the manufacturer while keeping EUR 25,000 as profit. Which type of L/C allows this?
opts: A. Back-to-Back L/C
B. Transferable L/C
C. Revolving L/C
D. Standby L/C
questionBank.exp: A Transferable L/C allows the first beneficiary (middleman) to transfer part or all of the credit to secondary beneficiaries (suppliers). The first beneficiary can substitute its own invoices and keep the difference. (Module 3.4, Transferable L/C)

questionBank.q: A middleman receives a Transferable L/C and requests the transferring bank to transfer EUR 75,000 to the manufacturer. The manufacturer (second beneficiary) ships goods and presents documents for EUR 75,000. The transferring bank notifies the middleman. The middleman substitutes its own invoice for EUR 100,000 and presents it. The bank pays the middleman EUR 100,000 and the manufacturer EUR 75,000. The middleman's profit is:
questionBank.exp: The middleman (first beneficiary) receives EUR 100,000 from the bank and pays the manufacturer EUR 75,000, keeping EUR 25,000 as profit. This is the classic transferable L/C mechanism. (Module 3.4, Transferable L/C, and sample case study)

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a unique feature of a Transferable L/C compared to a Back-to-Back L/C?
opts: A. The first beneficiary can substitute its own documents
B. The first beneficiary must open a separate L/C
C. The second beneficiary must be identified in the original L/C
D. The original L/C must be confirmed
questionBank.exp: In a Transferable L/C, the first beneficiary can substitute its own invoice and draft for those of the second beneficiary. This is a key feature that differentiates it from Back-to-Back L/Cs. (Module 3.4, Transferable L/C vs Back-to-Back L/C)

questionBank.q: A middleman receives an L/C from a buyer but the L/C is not marked 'Transferable'. The middleman wants to source goods from a supplier. The middleman can:
opts: A. Still transfer the L/C because all L/Cs are transferable
B. Not transfer the L/C because it must state it is transferable
C. Transfer the L/C with the buyer's verbal consent
D. Use the L/C as collateral to open a Back-to-Back L/C
questionBank.exp: If an L/C is not marked 'Transferable', it cannot be transferred. The middleman can instead use the original L/C as collateral to open a Back-to-Back L/C with a supplier. (Module 3.4, Back-to-Back L/C)

questionBank.q: In a Back-to-Back L/C arrangement, how many distinct L/Cs are issued?
opts: A. One L/C
B. Two L/Cs (Prime and Secondary)
C. Three L/Cs
D. The same L/C is reused
questionBank.exp: A Back-to-Back L/C involves two separate L/Cs: the Prime (or Master) L/C issued in favour of the middleman, and the Secondary L/C issued by the middleman's bank in favour of the supplier. These are two distinct transactions. (Module 3.4, Back-to-Back L/C)

questionBank.q: A buyer in the UK issues an L/C for EUR 100,000 in favour of a middleman in Germany. The middleman uses this L/C as security to open a second L/C for EUR 75,000 in favour of a manufacturer in China. The manufacturer ships goods and presents documents. The middleman's bank pays the manufacturer EUR 75,000. The middleman then presents documents under the Prime L/C and receives EUR 100,000. The middleman keeps EUR 25,000. This arrangement is a:
opts: A. Transferable L/C
B. Back-to-Back L/C
C. Revolving L/C
D. Standby L/C
questionBank.exp: This is a Back-to-Back L/C arrangement. Two separate L/Cs are issued: the Prime L/C from the buyer to the middleman, and the Secondary L/C from the middleman's bank to the manufacturer. (Module 3.4, Back-to-Back L/C)

questionBank.q: Which of the following is a risk specific to the first beneficiary in a Back-to-Back L/C arrangement?
opts: A. The secondary beneficiary may not perform
B. The prime L/C may be amended without consent
C. The issuing bank may refuse the prime L/C
D. The buyer may reject the goods
questionBank.exp: In a Back-to-Back L/C, the first beneficiary (middleman) bears the performance risk of the secondary beneficiary (supplier). If the supplier fails to ship conforming goods, the middleman cannot present documents under the Prime L/C. (Module 3.7, Back-to-Back L/C risks)

questionBank.q: A Transferable L/C can be transferred to:
opts: A. Only one secondary beneficiary
B. One or more secondary beneficiaries
C. Only the manufacturer
D. Only the buyer
questionBank.exp: A Transferable L/C can be transferred in parts or whole to one or more secondary beneficiaries. This allows the first beneficiary to source from multiple suppliers. (Module 3.4, Transferable L/C)

questionBank.q: Under a Transferable L/C, which of the following terms and conditions can typically be reduced or curtailed?
opts: A. The description of goods
B. The value, tenor, latest shipment date, and presentation period
C. The applicant's name
D. The place of expiry
questionBank.exp: In a Transferable L/C, the value, tenor, latest shipment date, and presentation period can be reduced or curtailed. The description of goods cannot be changed. (Module 3.4, Transferable L/C)

questionBank.q: A Transferable L/C and a Back-to-Back L/C both allow a middleman to operate. What is a key difference in the level of security for the parties?
opts: A. The Transferable L/C offers more security for all parties
B. The Back-to-Back L/C offers more security
C. Both offer identical security
D. Neither offers any security
questionBank.exp: The Transferable L/C offers more security for all parties because it is a single elongated transaction with the original applicant involved. The Back-to-Back L/C is riskier for all parties because it involves two separate L/Cs. (Module 3.4, Transferable L/C vs Back-to-Back L/C)

questionBank.q: A buyer imports raw materials monthly for a year. The buyer wants to avoid the cost of opening a new L/C for each shipment. The buyer should use a:
opts: A. Transferable L/C
B. Back-to-Back L/C
C. Revolving L/C
D. Standby L/C
questionBank.exp: A Revolving L/C is designed for regular, repeated shipments. It automatically renews after each drawdown, saving time and cost compared to opening multiple L/Cs. (Module 3.4, Revolving L/C)

questionBank.q: A Revolving L/C is cumulative. The L/C amount is USD 1,000,000, with four shipments of USD 250,000 each. In the first shipment, the exporter ships only USD 200,000. The shortfall of USD 50,000:
opts: A. Can be added to subsequent shipments
B. Cannot be added to subsequent shipments
C. Must be claimed immediately
D. Is forfeited
questionBank.exp: Under a cumulative Revolving L/C, any shortfall in one shipment can be added to subsequent shipments within the prescribed period. This is the defining feature of cumulative revolving L/Cs. (Module 3.4, Revolving L/C)

questionBank.q: A Revolving L/C is non-cumulative. The L/C amount is USD 1,000,000, with four shipments of USD 250,000 each. In the first shipment, the exporter ships only USD 200,000. The shortfall of USD 50,000:
opts: A. Can be added to subsequent shipments
B. Cannot be added to subsequent shipments
C. Must be claimed immediately
D. Is refunded to the buyer
questionBank.exp: Under a non-cumulative Revolving L/C, shortfalls in one shipment cannot be made up in subsequent months. Each shipment is treated independently. This is a key distinction from cumulative L/Cs. (Module 3.4, Revolving L/C)

questionBank.q: A buyer has a Revolving L/C with a total value of USD 1,000,000, revolving monthly for 10 months at USD 100,000 per month. The L/C is cumulative. In the first month, the seller ships USD 80,000. In the second month, the seller ships USD 120,000. This is:
opts: A. Permitted because the cumulative shortfall of USD 20,000 can be added
B. Permitted because the L/C is cumulative
C. Permitted because the L/C value is not exceeded
D. Not permitted because the second shipment exceeds the monthly limit
questionBank.exp: Even under a cumulative L/C, no single shipment can exceed the periodic limit (unless the L/C allows). The second shipment of USD 120,000 exceeds the USD 100,000 monthly limit, so it would be a discrepancy. The shortfall can be added, but the monthly cap still applies. (Module 3.4, Revolving L/C)

questionBank.q: A Standby Letter of Credit is issued in favour of a seller to guarantee payment if the buyer defaults. The buyer makes all payments on time. The Standby L/C expires unused. The buyer's cost for this arrangement was:
opts: A. Zero, because the L/C was not used
B. The issuance fees and any confirmation charges
C. Refunded by the bank
D. Paid by the seller
questionBank.exp: A Standby L/C incurs fees regardless of whether it is drawn upon. The buyer pays the issuance fees (and potentially confirmation charges) even if the L/C expires unused. (Module 3.4, Standby L/C)

questionBank.q: A buyer in Nigeria issues a Standby L/C to guarantee payment to a seller in the UK. The seller is concerned about the issuing bank's credit. The seller requests that the Standby L/C be confirmed. This means:
opts: A. The seller will have two banks' undertakings
B. The seller must pay higher fees
C. The L/C becomes transferable
D. The L/C can be drawn at sight
questionBank.exp: If a Standby L/C is confirmed, the seller has the undertaking of both the issuing bank and the confirming bank. This is an extra layer of security. (Module 3.4, Confirmed L/C)

questionBank.q: A bank has received a request to issue a Standby L/C for a customer. The bank is concerned about the risk of the customer defaulting. Which risk is the bank primarily assessing?
opts: A. The beneficiary's credit risk
B. The applicant's credit risk
C. The country risk of the beneficiary
D. The performance risk of the carrier
